lessonRef.subject: mathematics
lessonRef.title: Investigation or close reading: populations and samples

sections.title: Instructional examples
sections.directions: This example shows the kind of reasoning the investigation asks for.

items.prompt: A researcher wants to know about all 400 students at Lincoln Middle School. She randomly selects 40 of them to survey. What is the sample in this situation?

steps: The population is every member of the group being studied: all 400 students.
The sample is the subset actually surveyed: the 40 randomly selected students.
workedSolution.answer: The 40 randomly selected students at Lincoln Middle School

sections.title: Guided practice
sections.directions: Talk through what changes and what stays fixed before you answer.

items.prompt: A student uses a random number generator to select 37 commuters on a train line from the full list, then surveys them. Is this sampling method likely to produce a representative sample?
choices: Yes, likely representative, because the sample size is large enough.
Yes, likely representative — every member had a fair, known chance of being chosen.
No, likely not representative — the method favors certain members over others.
No, likely not representative, because the population is too large.

items.prompt: In a random sample of 20 visitors to a science museum, 10 preferred an extended weekend event. Based on this sample, about how many of the 200 visitors to a science museum would you expect to prefer an extended weekend event?

sections.title: Independent practice
sections.directions: Work on your own. Show the steps that produced each answer.

items.prompt: Five random samples of the same population produced these mean scores: 23, 19, 22, 10, 12. What is the range of these sample estimates?

A population has 3093 shoppers at a grocery store. Student A takes a random sample of 34. Student B takes a random sample of 8. Both use proper random selection. Whose sample is more likely to give an estimate closer to the true population value?
choices: Both are equally likely to be accurate, because both are random.
Student A's sample of 34, because larger random samples tend to produce more consistent, accurate estimates.
Neither sample is reliable unless it includes the entire population.
Student B's sample of 8, because smaller samples are easier to analyze.

items.prompt: A student surveys 74 students at Lincoln Middle School using a convenience sample of her classmates only and records the results. Is it valid to generalize this result to all 2812 students at Lincoln Middle School?
choices: Yes, because the sample size is large enough regardless of how it was chosen.
Yes, because the sample was selected randomly, so it is likely representative of the population.
No, because samples can never be generalized to a population.
No, because the sample was not randomly selected, so it may not represent the population.

items.prompt: A sample of 7 values is: 66, 65, 56, 59, 59, 65, 63. What is the median of this data set?

sections.title: Extension and challenge
sections.directions: Write out the reasoning in full sentences. A correct answer with no justification does not count here.

items.prompt: A data set has 6 values: 32, 42, 33, 39, 40, 36. What is the new mean if an outlier of 85 is added to the data set, making 7 values in all?
items.responseExpectation: Give the result and the reasoning that produced it. Show enough work that someone else could check each step.

items.prompt: A data set is: 11, 17, 30, 24, 23, with a mean of 21. What is the mean absolute deviation (MAD) of this data set?
items.responseExpectation: Give the result and the reasoning that produced it. Show enough work that someone else could check each step.
